---
title: "Homework 6: Wind Turbine Siting in Iowa"
---

## Overview

For this assignment you will create a well-designed knitted .html report that analyzes how the locations of wind turbines in Iowa have changed over time.

## Scenario

You are an analyst for the Iowa Economic Development Authority. Iowa gets more of its electricity from wind than almost any other state, and the Authority wants to understand how turbine siting has changed as the industry has grown. You have been asked to look at patterns in the location and density of wind turbines across Iowa and to create a cohesive document for the Authority's board about these patterns and how they changed over time.

The data include the location of every wind turbine in Iowa from the [U.S. Wind Turbine Database](https://energy.usgs.gov/uswtdb/), with the year its project came online (`p_year`). Compare two periods: turbines built before 2012 and turbines built in 2012 or later.

## Task

The report should integrate narrative interpretation, spatial analysis, and visualizations to describe how wind turbines are distributed across Iowa and how these patterns differ between the two periods. For each period, use point pattern analysis to evaluate first-order and second-order spatial structure. Connect the observed patterns to features of Iowa's landscape and infrastructure, such as wind resources, transmission lines, farmland, or population centers, and state clear hypotheses about the processes generating the patterns.

Then compare the two periods to assess how the spatial structure of turbine siting has changed, including shifts in intensity, clustering, or spatial concentration. Ground this comparison in contextual changes, supported by external research on factors such as federal tax credits, utility investment, larger turbine technology, transmission expansion, or local siting rules. You may need additional visualizations (such as a tmap with a basemap) for the comparison.

**Window and units.** Use the Iowa outline as the window for your point patterns (`as.owin(iowa)`). Both files are projected to UTM zone 15N, so distances are in meters.

**Duplicate locations.** A handful of turbines share exact coordinates, and nearest-neighbor distances of zero break the nearest-neighbor and K/L-function analyses. Before the second-order analysis, analyze the unique locations with `unique()`, or jitter the points slightly with `rjitter()`.

## Data

In your .Rmd, add a chunk for loading libraries and reading in data, and paste in this code:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
#load libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(tmap)
library(maptiles)
library(spatstat)
library(sf)

#wind turbines in Iowa (CRS units are meters)
turbines <- st_read("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jucardwell/geog391/main/data/iowa_wind_turbines.geojson")

#Iowa outline, to use as the window
iowa <- st_read("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jucardwell/geog391/main/data/iowa_boundary.geojson")

#the two periods
early_period <- turbines |> filter(p_year < 2012)
late_period <- turbines |> filter(p_year >= 2012)
```

Submit your polished knitted .html to the Homework 6 assignment on Canvas.

## Rubric (10 Points)

| Part | Points | Criteria |
|---|---|---|
| Analysis and visualizations | 4 | Correctly applies point pattern analysis to both periods, with clear interpretation of first-order and second-order structure for each (2); appropriate, well-designed visualizations that support interpretation and comparison (2) |
| Discussion | 6 | Explains turbine siting patterns and change over time in plain language for a policy audience (2); compares the periods with plausible, evidence-based explanations grounded in Iowa context and external research (2); integrates analysis, visualizations and interpretation into a cohesive, well-structured report with citations (2) |
